subject: math
title: Dividing by Two-Digit Numbers
seo_title: Grade 5 Dividing by Two-Digit Numbers Worksheets: Area Model, Long Division, Remainders (Free, Ontario)
standard_text: Represent and solve problems involving the division of three-digit whole numbers by two-digit whole numbers using the area model and using algorithms, and make connections between the two methods, while expressing any remainder appropriately
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 math worksheets on dividing three-digit numbers by two-digit numbers for the Ontario curriculum: multiples of 10, the area model, long division, remainders as whole numbers, fractions or rounded up, and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Round the divisor to estimate each digit, then check it. The remainder is always less than the divisor.
key_sub: 672 ÷ 32: the area model splits 672 into 640 + 32, so the answer is 20 + 1 = 21. In a story, decide what the remainder means: round up for buses, leave it out for full boxes, or write it as a fraction.
body_html:
The big idea

Dividing asks: how many groups of the divisor fit into the number? With a two-digit divisor, you estimate first. Round the divisor to the nearest ten, try a digit, then check it.

Divide by multiples of 10

Use a basic fact. Cross out one 0 in each number: 240 ÷ 30 = 24 ÷ 3 = 8. If the dividend has two zeros, keep one in the answer: 600 ÷ 20 = 60 ÷ 2 = 30.

Estimate

Estimate 243 ÷ 31.

Round 31 to 30. 240 is close to 243, and 24 ÷ 3 = 8, so 240 ÷ 30 = 8.

Answer: about 8 (exactly 7 R 26)

The area model

Draw a rectangle with the divisor on the side. Split the dividend into parts that are easy multiples of the divisor, like 10 or 20 times. Divide each part, then add the tops.

Long division

Long division does the same work in place-value order: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.

The two methods match: the 2 in the tens place is the 20 part of the area model, and the 640 in the area model is the 64 tens in long division.

Remainders

The remainder is what is left when no more full groups fit. It is always less than the divisor.

In a story, decide what the remainder means.

The question asksUse the remainder like this230 students, 48 on each bus
How many are needed for everyone?Round up: add 15 buses
How many full groups?Leave the remainder out4 full buses
How many are left over?The remainder is the answer38 students

If the leftovers can be split, like metres of rope or litres of water, write the remainder as a fraction of the divisor: 125 ÷ 12 = 10 R 5 = 10 512.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Ignoring the remainder (230 students need 4 buses)4 buses leave 38 students behind: 5 buses
First digit in the wrong place (192 ÷ 48 = 40)19 is less than 48, so start above the ones: 4
Losing a 0 (720 ÷ 24 = 3)Every place after the first needs a digit: 30
A remainder that is too big (230 ÷ 48 = 3 R 86)86 is more than 48, so one more group fits: 4 R 38
Writing the remainder as a decimal (125 ÷ 12 = 10.5)R 5 means 5 out of 12: 10 512

faq.q: What division do Grade 5 students learn in Ontario?
faq.a: The Ontario math curriculum asks Grade 5 students to divide three-digit whole numbers by two-digit whole numbers, using the area model and long division, and to show the remainder in a way that fits the problem.

faq.q: How do you divide by a two-digit number?
faq.a: Round the divisor to the nearest ten to estimate each digit, then multiply, subtract and bring down the next digit. If the product is too big, try one less; if what is left is the divisor or more, try one more.

faq.q: How does the area model help with division?
faq.a: It splits the dividend into easy parts, such as 32 × 20 = 640 and 32 × 1 = 32 for 672 ÷ 32. Adding the parts on top (20 + 1 = 21) gives the quotient, and it shows why long division works.

faq.q: What should you do with a remainder in a word problem?
faq.a: Round up when everyone must fit, like students on buses. Leave it out when you count full boxes, give the remainder when the question asks what is left, and write it as a fraction when the leftovers can be split.

items.q: What number goes in the box? ☐ × 60 = 480
items.e: Think: what number times 60 is 480? That is 480 ÷ 60 = 48 ÷ 6 = 8. Check: 8 × 60 = 480.

items.q: What number goes in the box? ☐ × 80 = 240
items.e: Think: what number times 80 is 240? That is 240 ÷ 80 = 24 ÷ 8 = 3. Check: 3 × 80 = 240.

items.q: What number goes in the box? ☐ × 70 = 280
items.e: Think: what number times 70 is 280? That is 280 ÷ 70 = 28 ÷ 7 = 4. Check: 4 × 70 = 280.

items.q: What is 160 ÷ 80?
items.e: Think of the fact: 16 ÷ 8 = 2. Cross out one 0 in each number: 160 ÷ 80 = 16 ÷ 8 = 2. Check: 2 × 80 = 160.

items.q: Round the divisor to the nearest ten to estimate 267 ÷ 31.
items.e: Round 31 to 30. 267 is close to 270, and 27 ÷ 3 = 9, so 270 ÷ 30 = 9. 267 ÷ 31 is about 9. (The exact answer is 8 R 19.)

items.q: What is 490 ÷ 70?
items.e: Think of the fact: 49 ÷ 7 = 7. Cross out one 0 in each number: 490 ÷ 70 = 49 ÷ 7 = 7. Check: 7 × 70 = 490.

items.q: Round the divisor to the nearest ten to estimate 307 ÷ 49.
items.e: Round 49 to 50. 307 is close to 300, and 30 ÷ 5 = 6, so 300 ÷ 50 = 6. 307 ÷ 49 is about 6. (The exact answer is 6 R 13.)

items.q: What is 600 ÷ 20?
items.e: Cross out one 0 in each number: 600 ÷ 20 = 60 ÷ 2. 6 ÷ 2 = 3, so 60 ÷ 2 = 30. Do not lose the 0 in the answer: 30 × 20 = 600.

items.q: What is 560 ÷ 70?
items.e: Think of the fact: 56 ÷ 7 = 8. Cross out one 0 in each number: 560 ÷ 70 = 56 ÷ 7 = 8. Check: 8 × 70 = 560.

items.q: What is 170 ÷ 70?
items.e: 2 × 70 = 140 and 3 × 70 = 210, which is too big. So 2 groups of 70 fit, and 170 − 140 = 30 is left. 170 ÷ 70 = 2 R 30. The remainder is 30, not 3: crossing out zeros does not change what is left over. Check: 2 × 70 + 30 = 170.

items.q: What is 150 ÷ 30?
items.e: Think of the fact: 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Cross out one 0 in each number: 150 ÷ 30 = 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Check: 5 × 30 = 150.

items.q: Round the divisor to the nearest ten to estimate 163 ÷ 42.
items.e: Round 42 to 40. 163 is close to 160, and 16 ÷ 4 = 4, so 160 ÷ 40 = 4. 163 ÷ 42 is about 4. (The exact answer is 3 R 37.)

items.q: What is 180 ÷ 90?
items.e: Think of the fact: 18 ÷ 9 = 2. Cross out one 0 in each number: 180 ÷ 90 = 18 ÷ 9 = 2. Check: 2 × 90 = 180.

items.q: What is 430 ÷ 80?
items.e: 5 × 80 = 400 and 6 × 80 = 480, which is too big. So 5 groups of 80 fit, and 430 − 400 = 30 is left. 430 ÷ 80 = 5 R 30. The remainder is 30, not 3: crossing out zeros does not change what is left over. Check: 5 × 80 + 30 = 430.

items.q: What is 360 ÷ 90?
items.e: Think of the fact: 36 ÷ 9 = 4. Cross out one 0 in each number: 360 ÷ 90 = 36 ÷ 9 = 4. Check: 4 × 90 = 360.

items.q: What is 800 ÷ 40?
items.e: Cross out one 0 in each number: 800 ÷ 40 = 80 ÷ 4. 8 ÷ 4 = 2, so 80 ÷ 4 = 20. Do not lose the 0 in the answer: 20 × 40 = 800.

items.q: Round the divisor to the nearest ten to estimate 482 ÷ 82.
items.e: Round 82 to 80. 482 is close to 480, and 48 ÷ 8 = 6, so 480 ÷ 80 = 6. 482 ÷ 82 is about 6. (The exact answer is 5 R 72.)

items.q: What is 270 ÷ 30?
items.e: Think of the fact: 27 ÷ 3 = 9. Cross out one 0 in each number: 270 ÷ 30 = 27 ÷ 3 = 9. Check: 9 × 30 = 270.

items.q: What is 710 ÷ 90?
items.e: 7 × 90 = 630 and 8 × 90 = 720, which is too big. So 7 groups of 90 fit, and 710 − 630 = 80 is left. 710 ÷ 90 = 7 R 80. The remainder is 80, not 8: crossing out zeros does not change what is left over. Check: 7 × 90 + 80 = 710.

items.q: What is 900 ÷ 30?
items.e: Cross out one 0 in each number: 900 ÷ 30 = 90 ÷ 3. 9 ÷ 3 = 3, so 90 ÷ 3 = 30. Do not lose the 0 in the answer: 30 × 30 = 900.

items.q: The area model shows 754 ÷ 26. What is the missing area (the red question mark)?
items.e: The area of a part is side × top: 26 × 20 = 520. Check: 520 + 234 = 754, and 754 ÷ 26 = 29.

items.q: The area model shows 377 ÷ 29. What number goes in place of the red question mark?
items.e: The part has area 87 and side 29. 87 ÷ 29 = 3, because 3 × 29 = 87. So 377 ÷ 29 = 10 + 3 = 13.

items.q: Use the area model to find 323 ÷ 17.
items.e: Each part is 17 × something. Divide each part by 17: 170 ÷ 17 = 10, 153 ÷ 17 = 9. Add the partial quotients: 10 + 9 = 19. Check: 19 × 17 = 323.

items.q: Use the area model to find 675 ÷ 45.
items.e: Each part is 45 × something. Divide each part by 45: 450 ÷ 45 = 10, 225 ÷ 45 = 5. Add the partial quotients: 10 + 5 = 15. Check: 15 × 45 = 675.

items.q: The area model shows 406 ÷ 14. What number goes in place of the red question mark?
items.e: The part has area 126 and side 14. 126 ÷ 14 = 9, because 9 × 14 = 126. So 406 ÷ 14 = 20 + 9 = 29.

items.q: Mr. Tremblay uses this area model to divide 189 ÷ 15. What is 189 ÷ 15?
items.e: The model uses 150 + 30 = 180. 189 − 180 = 9 is left, and 9 is less than 15, so it is the remainder. 189 ÷ 15 = 12 R 9. Check: 12 × 15 + 9 = 189.

items.q: You want to find 336 ÷ 28 with an area model. Which way to split 336 works best?
items.e: Each part must be a multiple of 28, so it divides with no remainder. 280 = 28 × 10 and 56 = 28 × 2. So 336 ÷ 28 = 10 + 2 = 12. Splitting by place value (300 + 36) does not work: 300 ÷ 28 is not a whole number.

items.q: The area model shows 513 ÷ 27. What is the missing area (the red question mark)?
items.e: The area of a part is side × top: 27 × 10 = 270. Check: 270 + 243 = 513, and 513 ÷ 27 = 19.

items.q: The area model shows 210 ÷ 15. What is the missing area (the red question mark)?
items.e: The area of a part is side × top: 15 × 10 = 150. Check: 150 + 60 = 210, and 210 ÷ 15 = 14.

items.q: Use the area model to find 432 ÷ 12.
items.e: Each part is 12 × something. Divide each part by 12: 120 ÷ 12 = 10, 120 ÷ 12 = 10, 120 ÷ 12 = 10, 72 ÷ 12 = 6. Add the partial quotients: 10 + 10 + 10 + 6 = 36. Check: 36 × 12 = 432.

items.q: Use the area model to find 416 ÷ 13.
items.e: Each part is 13 × something. Divide each part by 13: 390 ÷ 13 = 30, 26 ÷ 13 = 2. Add the partial quotients: 30 + 2 = 32. Check: 32 × 13 = 416.

items.q: Use the area model to find 864 ÷ 24.
items.e: Each part is 24 × something. Divide each part by 24: 240 ÷ 24 = 10, 240 ÷ 24 = 10, 240 ÷ 24 = 10, 144 ÷ 24 = 6. Add the partial quotients: 10 + 10 + 10 + 6 = 36. Check: 36 × 24 = 864.

items.q: Use the area model to find 450 ÷ 25.
items.e: Each part is 25 × something. Divide each part by 25: 250 ÷ 25 = 10, 200 ÷ 25 = 8. Add the partial quotients: 10 + 8 = 18. Check: 18 × 25 = 450.

items.q: Use the area model to find 288 ÷ 18.
items.e: Each part is 18 × something. Divide each part by 18: 180 ÷ 18 = 10, 108 ÷ 18 = 6. Add the partial quotients: 10 + 6 = 16. Check: 16 × 18 = 288.

items.q: Ms. Patel uses this area model to divide 424 ÷ 24. What is 424 ÷ 24?
items.e: The model uses 240 + 168 = 408. 424 − 408 = 16 is left, and 16 is less than 24, so it is the remainder. 424 ÷ 24 = 17 R 16. Check: 17 × 24 + 16 = 424.

items.q: You want to find 312 ÷ 26 with an area model. Which way to split 312 works best?
items.e: Each part must be a multiple of 26, so it divides with no remainder. 260 = 26 × 10 and 52 = 26 × 2. So 312 ÷ 26 = 10 + 2 = 12. Splitting by place value (300 + 12) does not work: 300 ÷ 26 is not a whole number.

items.q: The area model shows 272 ÷ 16. What number goes in place of the red question mark?
items.e: The part has area 112 and side 16. 112 ÷ 16 = 7, because 7 × 16 = 112. So 272 ÷ 16 = 10 + 7 = 17.

items.q: The area model shows 507 ÷ 39. What number goes in place of the red question mark?
items.e: The part has area 117 and side 39. 117 ÷ 39 = 3, because 3 × 39 = 117. So 507 ÷ 39 = 10 + 3 = 13.

items.q: You want to find 224 ÷ 16 with an area model. Which way to split 224 works best?
items.e: Each part must be a multiple of 16, so it divides with no remainder. 160 = 16 × 10 and 64 = 16 × 4. So 224 ÷ 16 = 10 + 4 = 14. Splitting by place value (200 + 24) does not work: 200 ÷ 16 is not a whole number.

items.q: Use the area model to find 532 ÷ 28.
items.e: Each part is 28 × something. Divide each part by 28: 280 ÷ 28 = 10, 252 ÷ 28 = 9. Add the partial quotients: 10 + 9 = 19. Check: 19 × 28 = 532.

items.q: What is 420 ÷ 14?
items.e: 4 is less than 14, so start with 42. 42 ÷ 14 is about 42 ÷ 10, so try 4. 4 × 14 = 56 is more than 42, so try 3. 3 × 14 = 42, 42 − 42 = 0. Bring down 0. Nothing is left to divide, so write 0. Answer: 30. Check: 30 × 14 = 420. The 0 in the ones place matters: 30 is not 3.

items.q: What is 390 ÷ 65?
items.e: 39 is less than 65, so start with 390. 390 ÷ 65 is about 390 ÷ 70, so try 5. 5 × 65 = 325 leaves 65, which is not less than 65, so try 6. 6 × 65 = 390, 390 − 390 = 0. Answer: 6. Check: 6 × 65 = 390.

items.q: Divide.
items.e: 9 is less than 28, so start with 95. 95 ÷ 28 is about 95 ÷ 30, so try 3. 3 × 28 = 84, 95 − 84 = 11. Bring down 2 to make 112. 112 ÷ 28 is about 112 ÷ 30, so try 3. 3 × 28 = 84 leaves 28, which is not less than 28, so try 4. 4 × 28 = 112, 112 − 112 = 0. Answer: 34. Check: 34 × 28 = 952.

items.q: Divide.
items.e: 10 is less than 25, so start with 100. 100 ÷ 25 is about 100 ÷ 30, so try 3. 3 × 25 = 75 leaves 25, which is not less than 25, so try 4. 4 × 25 = 100, 100 − 100 = 0. Answer: 4. Check: 4 × 25 = 100.

items.q: What is 395 ÷ 79?
items.e: 39 is less than 79, so start with 395. 395 ÷ 79 is about 395 ÷ 80, so try 4. 4 × 79 = 316 leaves 79, which is not less than 79, so try 5. 5 × 79 = 395, 395 − 395 = 0. Answer: 5. Check: 5 × 79 = 395.

items.q: What is 345 ÷ 15?
items.e: 3 is less than 15, so start with 34. 34 ÷ 15 is about 34 ÷ 20, so try 1. 1 × 15 = 15 leaves 19, which is not less than 15, so try 2. 2 × 15 = 30, 34 − 30 = 4. Bring down 5 to make 45. 45 ÷ 15 is about 45 ÷ 20, so try 2. 2 × 15 = 30 leaves 15, which is not less than 15, so try 3. 3 × 15 = 45, 45 − 45 = 0. Answer: 23. Check: 23 × 15 = 345.

items.q: Divide.
items.e: 7 is less than 15, so start with 73. 73 ÷ 15 is about 73 ÷ 20, so try 3. 3 × 15 = 45 leaves 28, which is not less than 15, so try 4. 4 × 15 = 60, 73 − 60 = 13. Bring down 5 to make 135. 9 × 15 = 135 and 10 × 15 = 150 is more than 135, so use 9. 135 − 135 = 0. Answer: 49. Check: 49 × 15 = 735.

items.q: Noah divides 352 ÷ 88. He rounds 88 to 90 and tries 3. 3 × 88 = 264 and 352 − 264 = 88. What should he do next?
items.e: 88 is not less than the divisor 88, so 88 fits one more time. Try 4: 4 × 88 = 352. So 352 ÷ 88 = 4.

items.q: What is 440 ÷ 22?
items.e: 4 is less than 22, so start with 44. 44 ÷ 22 is about 44 ÷ 20, so try 2. 2 × 22 = 44, 44 − 44 = 0. Bring down 0. Nothing is left to divide, so write 0. Answer: 20. Check: 20 × 22 = 440. The 0 in the ones place matters: 20 is not 2.

items.q: 713 ÷ 23 = 31. Which multiplication checks this answer?
items.e: Multiplication undoes division: quotient × divisor = dividend. 31 × 23 = 713, so the answer is right.

items.q: What is 608 ÷ 76?
items.e: 60 is less than 76, so start with 608. 608 ÷ 76 is about 608 ÷ 80, so try 7. 7 × 76 = 532 leaves 76, which is not less than 76, so try 8. 8 × 76 = 608, 608 − 608 = 0. Answer: 8. Check: 8 × 76 = 608.

items.q: What is 836 ÷ 44?
items.e: 8 is less than 44, so start with 83. 83 ÷ 44 is about 83 ÷ 40, so try 2. 2 × 44 = 88 is more than 83, so try 1. 1 × 44 = 44, 83 − 44 = 39. Bring down 6 to make 396. 396 ÷ 44 is about 396 ÷ 40, so try 9. 9 × 44 = 396, 396 − 396 = 0. Answer: 19. Check: 19 × 44 = 836.

items.q: Divide.
items.e: 54 is less than 91, so start with 546. 546 ÷ 91 is about 546 ÷ 90, so try 6. 6 × 91 = 546, 546 − 546 = 0. Answer: 6. Check: 6 × 91 = 546.

items.q: Mei divides 104 ÷ 13. She rounds 13 to 10 and tries 9. 9 × 13 = 117, which is more than 104. What should she do next?
items.e: 117 is more than 104, so 9 is too big. Try 8: 8 × 13 = 104. So 104 ÷ 13 = 8.

items.q: Divide.
items.e: 14 is less than 28, so start with 140. 140 ÷ 28 is about 140 ÷ 30, so try 4. 4 × 28 = 112 leaves 28, which is not less than 28, so try 5. 5 × 28 = 140, 140 − 140 = 0. Answer: 5. Check: 5 × 28 = 140.

items.q: Without dividing, how big is the answer to 444 ÷ 74?
items.e: The first two digits make 44, which is less than 74. So the quotient has no tens digit: it is a one-digit number. 444 ÷ 74 = 6.

items.q: Without dividing, how big is the answer to 720 ÷ 15?
items.e: The first two digits make 72, which is at least 15. So the quotient has a tens digit: it is a two-digit number. 720 ÷ 15 = 48.

items.q: Divide.
items.e: 7 is less than 24, so start with 79. 79 ÷ 24 is about 79 ÷ 20, so try 3. 3 × 24 = 72, 79 − 72 = 7. Bring down 2 to make 72. 72 ÷ 24 is about 72 ÷ 20, so try 3. 3 × 24 = 72, 72 − 72 = 0. Answer: 33. Check: 33 × 24 = 792.

items.q: What is 273 ÷ 21?
items.e: 2 is less than 21, so start with 27. 27 ÷ 21 is about 27 ÷ 20, so try 1. 1 × 21 = 21, 27 − 21 = 6. Bring down 3 to make 63. 63 ÷ 21 is about 63 ÷ 20, so try 3. 3 × 21 = 63, 63 − 63 = 0. Answer: 13. Check: 13 × 21 = 273.

items.q: What is 960 ÷ 24?
items.e: 9 is less than 24, so start with 96. 96 ÷ 24 is about 96 ÷ 20, so try 4. 4 × 24 = 96, 96 − 96 = 0. Bring down 0. Nothing is left to divide, so write 0. Answer: 40. Check: 40 × 24 = 960. The 0 in the ones place matters: 40 is not 4.

sets.title: Remainders: whole numbers, fractions or round up

items.q: Which story needs the answer rounded up to the next whole number?
c: 230 m of rope cut into 48 pieces
items.e: 230 ÷ 48 = 4 R 38. With 4 buses, 38 students still need a seat, so you need 5 buses. The cookies question asks for full boxes (4), the rope can be cut (a fraction), and the cards question asks for the remainder (38).

items.q: What is 624 ÷ 33?
items.e: 6 is less than 33, so start with 62. 62 ÷ 33 is about 62 ÷ 30, so try 2. 2 × 33 = 66 is more than 62, so try 1. 1 × 33 = 33, 62 − 33 = 29. Bring down 4 to make 294. 294 ÷ 33 is about 294 ÷ 30, so try 9. 9 × 33 = 297 is more than 294, so try 8. 8 × 33 = 264, 294 − 264 = 30. Answer: 18 R 30. Check: 18 × 33 + 30 = 624.

items.q: What is 186 ÷ 33?
items.e: 18 is less than 33, so start with 186. 186 ÷ 33 is about 186 ÷ 30, so try 6. 6 × 33 = 198 is more than 186, so try 5. 5 × 33 = 165, 186 − 165 = 21. Answer: 5 R 21. Check: 5 × 33 + 21 = 186.

items.q: Nathan says 751 ÷ 27 = 26 R 49. What mistake did he make?
c: The quotient is in the wrong place
items.e: The remainder must be less than the divisor. 49 is more than 27, so 27 fits one more time: 49 − 27 = 22. The answer is 27 R 22. Check: 27 × 27 + 22 = 751.

items.q: Divide.
items.e: 9 is less than 31, so start with 90. 90 ÷ 31 is about 90 ÷ 30, so try 3. 3 × 31 = 93 is more than 90, so try 2. 2 × 31 = 62, 90 − 62 = 28. Bring down 2 to make 282. 282 ÷ 31 is about 282 ÷ 30, so try 9. 9 × 31 = 279, 282 − 279 = 3. Answer: 29 R 3. Check: 29 × 31 + 3 = 902.

items.q: Divide.
items.e: 39 is less than 62, so start with 391. 391 ÷ 62 is about 391 ÷ 60, so try 6. 6 × 62 = 372, 391 − 372 = 19. Answer: 6 R 19. Check: 6 × 62 + 19 = 391.

items.q: Write the answer to 130 ÷ 20 as a mixed number.
items.e: 130 ÷ 20 = 6 R 10. Put the remainder over the divisor: 1020. 1020 = 12, so the answer is 6 12. (6 R 10 is not 6.10.)

items.q: Write the answer to 125 ÷ 12 as a mixed number.
items.e: 125 ÷ 12 = 10 R 5. Put the remainder over the divisor: 512. The answer is 10 512. (10 R 5 is not 10.5.)

items.q: What is 427 ÷ 29?
items.e: 4 is less than 29, so start with 42. 42 ÷ 29 is about 42 ÷ 30, so try 1. 1 × 29 = 29, 42 − 29 = 13. Bring down 7 to make 137. 137 ÷ 29 is about 137 ÷ 30, so try 4. 4 × 29 = 116, 137 − 116 = 21. Answer: 14 R 21. Check: 14 × 29 + 21 = 427.

items.q: You divide a number by 24. Which of these could be the remainder?
items.e: A remainder is always less than the divisor. When you divide by 24, the remainder can be 0 to 23. So 23 is the only possible one.

items.q: Write the answer to 137 ÷ 11 as a mixed number.
items.e: 137 ÷ 11 = 12 R 5. Put the remainder over the divisor: 511. The answer is 12 511. (12 R 5 is not 12.5.)

items.q: 150 hockey players come to a tournament. Each change room holds 16 players. How many change rooms are needed?
items.e: 150 ÷ 16 = 9 R 6. 9 change rooms hold 144 players, so 6 players still need a place. Round up: 10 change rooms.

items.q: Write the answer to 290 ÷ 60 as a mixed number.
items.e: 290 ÷ 60 = 4 R 50. Put the remainder over the divisor: 5060. 5060 = 56, so the answer is 4 56. (4 R 50 is not 4.50.)

items.q: Arjun says 678 ÷ 73 = 90 R 21. What mistake did he make?
c: The quotient is in the wrong place
items.e: 67 is less than 73, so there are no tens in the quotient. The first digit goes above the ones place. 90 × 73 = 6570, not 678. The answer is 9 R 21.

items.q: 290 people come to a school concert. Each row has 24 chairs. How many rows are needed so everyone has a seat?
items.e: 290 ÷ 24 = 12 R 2. 12 rows hold 288 people, so 2 people still need a place. Round up: 13 rows.

items.q: Divide.
items.e: 22 is less than 51, so start with 223. 223 ÷ 51 is about 223 ÷ 50, so try 4. 4 × 51 = 204, 223 − 204 = 19. Answer: 4 R 19. Check: 4 × 51 + 19 = 223.

items.q: Which story uses a fraction for the remainder?
c: 125 L of water shared by 12 tanks
items.e: Water can be split into any amount, so each tank gets 10 512 L: 125 ÷ 12 = 10 R 5. You cannot split a hiker, an egg or a student, so those remainders stay whole numbers.

items.q: Write the answer to 163 ÷ 10 as a mixed number.
items.e: 163 ÷ 10 = 16 R 3. Put the remainder over the divisor: 310. The answer is 16 310.

items.q: Amira says 622 ÷ 36 = 17. What mistake did she make?
c: The quotient is in the wrong place
items.e: 17 × 36 = 612, not 622. 622 − 612 = 10 is left over, so the answer is 17 R 10.

items.q: Which story uses the remainder as the answer?
c: How many cards are not in a full pile?
How many piles are needed for all the cards?
How many piles can be filled?
How many cards are in each full pile?
items.e: “Not in a full pile” means the cards left over, which is the remainder. Full piles use the quotient, and “all the cards” means rounding up.

sets.title: Word problems: buses, boxes and more

items.q: 118 students visit the CN Tower. Each tour group can have up to 15 students. How many tour groups are needed?
items.e: 11 is less than 15, so start with 118. 7 × 15 = 105 and 8 × 15 = 120 is more than 118, so use 7. 118 − 105 = 13. So 118 ÷ 15 = 7 R 13. 7 tour groups are not enough: 13 students still need a group. Round up to 8 tour groups.

items.q: A 125 m rope is cut into 12 equal pieces for a canoe trip. How long is each piece?
items.e: 125 ÷ 12 = 10 R 5. The 5 m left over can be split too, so each one gets 512 m more. Answer: 10 512 m. (10 R 5 is not 10.5.)

items.q: A camp pours 137 L of water equally into 11 coolers. How much water is in each cooler?
items.e: 137 ÷ 11 = 12 R 5. The 5 L left over can be split too, so each one gets 511 L more. Answer: 12 511 L. (12 R 5 is not 12.5.)

items.q: A farm collects 315 eggs. The eggs go in cartons of 12. How many cartons can the farm fill?
items.e: 3 is less than 12, so start with 31. 31 ÷ 12 is about 31 ÷ 10, so try 3. 3 × 12 = 36 is more than 31, so try 2. 2 × 12 = 24, 31 − 24 = 7. Bring down 5 to make 75. 75 ÷ 12 is about 75 ÷ 10, so try 7. 7 × 12 = 84 is more than 75, so try 6. 6 × 12 = 72, 75 − 72 = 3. So 315 ÷ 12 = 26 R 3. The 3 eggs left over cannot fill another carton. The answer is 26 cartons.

items.q: A hockey arena has 864 seats in 32 equal rows. How many seats are in each row?
items.e: Share equally, so divide: 8 is less than 32, so start with 86. 86 ÷ 32 is about 86 ÷ 30, so try 2. 2 × 32 = 64, 86 − 64 = 22. Bring down 4 to make 224. 224 ÷ 32 is about 224 ÷ 30, so try 7. 7 × 32 = 224, 224 − 224 = 0. So 864 ÷ 32 = 27. Check: 27 × 32 = 864.

items.q: A school board takes 410 students to a play in Toronto. Each school bus holds 72 students. How many buses are needed?
items.e: 41 is less than 72, so start with 410. 410 ÷ 72 is about 410 ÷ 70, so try 5. 5 × 72 = 360, 410 − 360 = 50. So 410 ÷ 72 = 5 R 50. 5 buses are not enough: 50 students still need a seat. Round up to 6 buses.

items.q: Hana has 400 hockey cards. She puts them in piles of 36. How many cards are not in a full pile?
items.e: 4 is less than 36, so start with 40. 40 ÷ 36 is about 40 ÷ 40, so try 1. 1 × 36 = 36, 40 − 36 = 4. Bring down 0 to make 40. 40 ÷ 36 is about 40 ÷ 40, so try 1. 1 × 36 = 36, 40 − 36 = 4. So 400 ÷ 36 = 11 R 4. The question asks what is left over. That is the remainder: 4 cards.

items.q: A bakery makes 470 butter tarts. It packs them in boxes of 24. How many boxes can it fill completely?
items.e: 4 is less than 24, so start with 47. 47 ÷ 24 is about 47 ÷ 20, so try 2. 2 × 24 = 48 is more than 47, so try 1. 1 × 24 = 24, 47 − 24 = 23. Bring down 0 to make 230. 230 ÷ 24 is about 230 ÷ 20, so try 9. 9 × 24 = 216, 230 − 216 = 14. So 470 ÷ 24 = 19 R 14. The 14 tarts left over cannot fill another box. The answer is 19 boxes.

items.q: 340 students go to a hockey game. Each bus holds 52 students. Maya says 6 buses are enough because 340 ÷ 52 = 6 R 28. Is she right?
items.e: 6 buses hold 6 × 52 = 312 students. 340 − 312 = 28 students would have no seat, so one more bus is needed: 7 buses.

items.q: Ava has $250 to buy hockey tickets for a class trip. Each ticket costs $18. How many tickets can she buy?
items.e: 2 is less than 18, so start with 25. 25 ÷ 18 is about 25 ÷ 20, so try 1. 1 × 18 = 18, 25 − 18 = 7. Bring down 0 to make 70. 70 ÷ 18 is about 70 ÷ 20, so try 3. 3 × 18 = 54, 70 − 54 = 16. So 250 ÷ 18 = 13 R 16. The $16 left over is not enough for another ticket. The answer is 13 tickets.

items.q: A sugar bush makes 345 L of maple syrup. It fills 15 big pails with the same amount. How much syrup is in each pail?
items.e: Share equally, so divide: 3 is less than 15, so start with 34. 34 ÷ 15 is about 34 ÷ 20, so try 1. 1 × 15 = 15 leaves 19, which is not less than 15, so try 2. 2 × 15 = 30, 34 − 30 = 4. Bring down 5 to make 45. 45 ÷ 15 is about 45 ÷ 20, so try 2. 2 × 15 = 30 leaves 15, which is not less than 15, so try 3. 3 × 15 = 45, 45 − 45 = 0. So 345 ÷ 15 = 23. Check: 23 × 15 = 345.

items.q: The gym has 340 chairs for a concert. They are set out in rows of 24. How many full rows are there?
items.e: 3 is less than 24, so start with 34. 34 ÷ 24 is about 34 ÷ 20, so try 1. 1 × 24 = 24, 34 − 24 = 10. Bring down 0 to make 100. 100 ÷ 24 is about 100 ÷ 20, so try 5. 5 × 24 = 120 is more than 100, so try 4. 4 × 24 = 96, 100 − 96 = 4. So 340 ÷ 24 = 14 R 4. The 4 chairs left over do not make another full row. The answer is 14 rows.

items.q: 230 students from a school go on a field trip. Each bus holds 48 students. How many buses are needed?
items.e: 23 is less than 48, so start with 230. 230 ÷ 48 is about 230 ÷ 50, so try 4. 4 × 48 = 192, 230 − 192 = 38. So 230 ÷ 48 = 4 R 38. 4 buses are not enough: 38 students still need a seat. Round up to 5 buses.

items.q: A school buys 6 boxes of 48 freezies. The freezies are shared equally among 24 classes. How many freezies does each class get?
items.e: Step 1: 6 × 48 = 288 freezies. Step 2: 2 is less than 24, so start with 28. 28 ÷ 24 is about 28 ÷ 20, so try 1. 1 × 24 = 24, 28 − 24 = 4. Bring down 8 to make 48. 48 ÷ 24 is about 48 ÷ 20, so try 2. 2 × 24 = 48, 48 − 48 = 0. So 288 ÷ 24 = 12. Each class gets 12 freezies.

items.q: For a soccer day, 156 students are put into teams of 12. Which number sentence finds the number of teams?
items.e: You know the total (156) and the size of each team (12), so divide the total by 12: 156 ÷ 12 = 13 teams. Check: 13 × 12 = 156. 12 ÷ 156 divides the wrong way: the total always comes first.

items.q: A teacher has 370 sheets of paper. She gives the same number to each of 28 students, as many as she can. How many sheets are left over?
items.e: 3 is less than 28, so start with 37. 37 ÷ 28 is about 37 ÷ 30, so try 1. 1 × 28 = 28, 37 − 28 = 9. Bring down 0 to make 90. 90 ÷ 28 is about 90 ÷ 30, so try 3. 3 × 28 = 84, 90 − 84 = 6. So 370 ÷ 28 = 13 R 6. The question asks what is left over. That is the remainder: 6 sheets.

items.q: For the Terry Fox Run, 18 classes raise $702 in all. Each class raises the same amount. How much does each class raise?
items.e: Share equally, so divide: 7 is less than 18, so start with 70. 70 ÷ 18 is about 70 ÷ 20, so try 3. 3 × 18 = 54, 70 − 54 = 16. Bring down 2 to make 162. 162 ÷ 18 is about 162 ÷ 20, so try 8. 8 × 18 = 144 leaves 18, which is not less than 18, so try 9. 9 × 18 = 162, 162 − 162 = 0. So 702 ÷ 18 = 39. Check: 39 × 18 = 702.

items.q: A school buys 528 pencils in boxes of 24. How many boxes does it buy?
items.e: Share equally, so divide: 5 is less than 24, so start with 52. 52 ÷ 24 is about 52 ÷ 20, so try 2. 2 × 24 = 48, 52 − 48 = 4. Bring down 8 to make 48. 48 ÷ 24 is about 48 ÷ 20, so try 2. 2 × 24 = 48, 48 − 48 = 0. So 528 ÷ 24 = 22. Check: 22 × 24 = 528.

items.q: Olivia's class raises $500 at a bake sale. They spend $68 on supplies and share the rest equally among 16 charities. How much does each charity get?
items.e: Step 1: $500 − $68 = $432. Step 2: 4 is less than 16, so start with 43. 43 ÷ 16 is about 43 ÷ 20, so try 2. 2 × 16 = 32, 43 − 32 = 11. Bring down 2 to make 112. 7 × 16 = 112 and 8 × 16 = 128 is more than 112, so use 7. 112 − 112 = 0. So 432 ÷ 16 = 27. Each charity gets $27. ($31 comes from dividing $500 by 16 and forgetting to take away the $68 first.)

items.q: A library is moving 650 books. Each box holds 28 books. How many boxes are needed to pack all the books?
items.e: 6 is less than 28, so start with 65. 65 ÷ 28 is about 65 ÷ 30, so try 2. 2 × 28 = 56, 65 − 56 = 9. Bring down 0 to make 90. 90 ÷ 28 is about 90 ÷ 30, so try 3. 3 × 28 = 84, 90 − 84 = 6. So 650 ÷ 28 = 23 R 6. 23 boxes are not enough: 6 books still need a box. Round up to 24 boxes.
